profile.reading:
TierPoint operates two data centers in the Tulsa, Oklahoma market, and this record carries the reference code TUL in the source map data without specifying which of the two it identifies. The older of the two, TierPoint Archer, sits at 322 East Archer Street in Tulsa's Brady Arts District, spanning more than 36,000 total square feet with more than 4,000 square feet of raised floor. The newer facility, TierPoint State Farm, sits at 12151 East State Farm Boulevard, spanning more than 32,000 total square feet with more than 16,000 square feet of raised floor, and is notably the only facility in this Oklahoma research batch to carry a disclosed Uptime Institute Tier III certification. TierPoint announced construction of this second Tulsa facility in May 2017, an initial roughly 20 million dollar phase built in partnership with Compass Data Centers, and completed construction on February 26, 2018, with a raised-floor figure matching the State Farm facility's current listing, making State Farm the more likely match for a newer, purpose-built site, though TierPoint's own announcements do not use either facility's name explicitly, leaving the TUL reference code unresolved between the two. Both facilities carry TierPoint's standard SOC 1 and SOC 2 Type II (including HITRUST), HIPAA, PCI-DSS, GLBA, and ISO 27001 compliance package. TierPoint, headquartered in St. Louis, Missouri, was formed in 2010 and now operates roughly 40 data centers across 20 US markets. As is standard industry practice, tenant identities are not publicly disclosed.

TierPoint has also grown through significant recent capital raises beyond its acquisition history: a 320 million dollar equity round in April 2020 led by Argo Infrastructure Partners, Wafra, and Macquarie Capital Principal Finance alongside existing investors, followed by Argo's 500 million dollar investment in February 2022 that made it TierPoint's largest single equity investor, and a further increase to Argo's ownership and capital commitment announced in December 2025. Jerry Kent, TierPoint's chairman and chief executive, also co-founded Charter Communications in 1993 and Cequel III in 2002, the entity that manages TierPoint, giving the company leadership deep roots in the broader telecommunications and cable infrastructure industry.
profile.research_note: TierPoint operates two named Tulsa facilities per its own site: Archer (322 E Archer St, 36,000+ sqft, older/original Tulsa facility in the Brady Arts District) and State Farm (12151 E State Farm Blvd, 32,000+ sqft, 16,000+ raised floor, Tier III certified -- the only Tulsa or Oklahoma facility in this research batch with a disclosed Uptime Institute tier). State Farm facility was announced May 2017 (~$20M initial phase, built with Compass Data Centers) and completed construction Feb 26 2018, with raised-floor figures matching current State Farm listing. Could not confirm which specific facility carries the OSM "TUL" ref code -- both are listed for honest disambiguation.

reading.body:
No power capacity is published for this TierPoint facility in Tulsa, so it cannot be sized against AI workloads or ranked within the state's data center portfolio.

The facility occupies 4,000 square feet of technical space and holds six certifications spanning enterprise audit, payment processing, healthcare, and defense compliance. This certification stack is the inverse of AI infrastructure: it describes a campus built for regulated colocation workloads that require proof of security controls, not one built for the thermal density and redundancy that large-scale compute demands. The absence of a published megawatt figure is consistent with this positioning.

Oklahoma reports nine mapped data center facilities with zero published megawatts across all of them. A single facility cannot be evaluated against state capacity or regional AI infrastructure trends when the baseline data does not exist. Tulsa remains invisible to the infrastructure constraints that now govern AI scaling decisions, not because the building is irrelevant to data centers in general, but because the operator has not disclosed the power figure that would make it legible to compute-constrained planning.
